regimes.name: Dot-com melt-up
regimes.fed_policy: Tightening: fed funds raised from 4.75% to 6.0% by March 2000 (final hike to 6.5% in May 2000).
regimes.summary: Internet, telecom-equipment and software stocks absorbed capital at any price while the Fed tightened into the top. The Nasdaq rose 85.6% in 1999 versus 21.0% for the S&P 500 and peaked on 10 March 2000 at 5,048.62. Old-economy value, utilities and materials were starved of flows.

regimes.name: Dot-com bust
regimes.fed_policy: Aggressive easing: surprise 50 bp cut to 6.0% on 3 January 2001, then down to 1.25% by November 2002.
regimes.summary: Technology fell 82.4% and telecom 74.1% peak-to-trough against 49.2% for the S&P 500, while staples gained 24%. Accounting scandals (Enron, WorldCom) and the 9/11 shock extended the bear; rate cuts could not revive capex, and capital rotated to defensives, small-cap value and housing-linked financials.

regimes.name: Reflation and credit boom
regimes.fed_policy: 1% floor (June 2003) then 17 'measured pace' hikes from 1.25% (30 June 2004) to 5.25% (29 June 2006); on hold until September 2007.
regimes.summary: A 2003 tech bounce (Nasdaq +50%) gave way to a commodity, emerging-market and housing-credit boom in which energy, materials, banks and utilities led and large-cap tech lagged (Nasdaq +1.4% in 2005). The iPhone launch in June 2007 arrived just as mortgage credit cracked.

regimes.name: Global financial crisis
regimes.fed_policy: Emergency easing from 5.25% to 0-0.25% (16 December 2008); QE1 agency/MBS purchases announced 25 November 2008.
regimes.summary: Financials fell 82.6% and materials 59.6% peak-to-trough against 56.8% for the S&P 500; tech (-53%) outperformed on cash-rich balance sheets and overtook financials as the largest sector in May 2008. Oil collapsed from $147 to $30 in five months. Only cash, Treasuries and quality balance sheets preserved capital.

regimes.name: QE recovery (QE1-QE3)
regimes.fed_policy: Zero rates throughout; QE2 ($600 billion, 3 November 2010), Operation Twist (2011), QE3 ($40 billion a month MBS, 13 September 2012).
regimes.summary: Stress tests (May 2009) ended the bank panic and the smartphone and cloud build-out led growth (Nasdaq +43.9% in 2009). The 2011 US downgrade and Eurozone crisis produced a mid-cycle defensive rotation (utilities +19.9%, financials -17.1% in 2011) before QE3 drove financials to the best sector in 2012 (+28.8%).

regimes.name: Taper tantrum and taper
regimes.fed_policy: Taper signalled 22 May 2013, purchases cut from $85 billion a month starting January 2014 (announced 18 December 2013), QE3 ended October 2014; rates still 0-0.25%.
regimes.summary: Bond proxies (utilities, REITs, telecom) were hit hard in mid-2013 as yields jumped, then recovered in 2014 as yields fell again (utilities +29.0% in 2014). Energy began its collapse in H2 2014 (-7.8%) while tech and health care led a 32.4% S&P 500 year in 2013.

regimes.name: Industrial recession and oil crash
regimes.fed_policy: Liftoff to 0.25-0.5% on 16 December 2015 after a year of delay; one hike only.
regimes.summary: China's August 2015 devaluation, oil below $30 and the Glencore scare drove a global industrial recession without a US one. Energy (-21.1%) and materials (-8.4%) lagged in 2015; large-cap growth and 'FANG' concentration began. Semiconductor M&A hit records as unit growth slowed.

regimes.name: Reflation, election and synchronized growth
regimes.fed_policy: Gradual hikes: three in 2017 to 1.25-1.5%; balance-sheet runoff began October 2017.
regimes.summary: Cyclicals led off the February 2016 low (energy +27.4%, materials +16.7% in 2016), the Trump election produced the best bank month on record (KBE +18.7% in November 2016) with tech lagging, and 2017's synchronized global growth and tax cut delivered a tech melt-up (+38.8%, FAANG +46.5%) with record-low volatility.

regimes.name: Hiking cycle and trade war
regimes.fed_policy: Four hikes to 2.25-2.5% (final on 19 December 2018) plus QT at $50 billion a month.
regimes.summary: Steel tariffs (March), Section 301 tariffs on China and four Fed hikes ended the low-volatility regime. Materials (-14.7%), financials (-13.0%) and energy (-18.1%) lagged; the GICS Communication Services sector was created in September; Q4 brought the worst December since 1931 (Nasdaq -17.5% for the quarter) and a Nasdaq-100 bear market.

sources.title: US stocks post worst year in a decade (CNBC, 2018-12-31)

regimes.name: Fed pivot and late-cycle growth
regimes.fed_policy: Pause in January 2019, three cuts to 1.5-1.75% (31 July, 18 September, 30 October 2019); QT ended August 2019; repo/bill purchases from October 2019.
regimes.summary: The Fed's reversal re-rated long-duration growth: technology returned 50.3% in 2019 (best sector) against 31.5% for the S&P 500, semiconductors led despite the May 2019 Huawei shock, and the Phase One trade deal (15 January 2020) removed the tariff overhang just before COVID.

regimes.name: COVID crash
regimes.fed_policy: Emergency cuts to 0-0.25% (3 and 15 March 2020), $700 billion QE announced 15 March, unlimited QE and credit facilities from 23 March.
regimes.summary: The fastest bear market on record: the Dow fell 12.93% on 16 March alone. Energy, airlines, banks and REITs were hit hardest; digital, staples and health care held up. The crash ended on 23 March once the Fed backstopped credit markets and Congress passed the CARES Act.

regimes.name: Reopening, reflation and the everything rally
regimes.fed_policy: Zero rates and $120 billion a month QE; taper announced November 2021 and accelerated December 2021.
regimes.summary: 2020 belonged to work-from-home tech (IT +43.9%, Nasdaq +43.6%); 2021 to reflation (energy +54.6%, financials +35.0%, materials +27.3%) as vaccines, fiscal stimulus and the chip shortage lifted cyclicals, while SPACs, fintech and crypto (Coinbase listing April 2021) marked the speculative peak. Utilities (+17.7%) were the 2021 laggard.

regimes.name: 2022 tightening bear market
regimes.fed_policy: Liftoff 16 March 2022 (0.25-0.5%), four 75 bp hikes, 3.0-3.25% by September and 4.25-4.5% by December; QT from June 2022.
regimes.summary: The fastest hiking cycle in four decades repriced duration: the S&P 500 fell about 25% to its October low and -18.1% for the year, with communication services -39.9% and technology -28.2% against energy +65.7% and utilities +1.6%. Software and fintech halved; Meta and Netflix posted record one-day losses; the growth-to-value rotation was the largest since 2000.

regimes.name: AI trade and soft landing, higher for longer
regimes.fed_policy: Final hikes to 5.25-5.5% (26 July 2023), then a 14-month hold; QT continuing.
regimes.summary: ChatGPT (30 November 2022) and Nvidia's May 2023 guidance ignited the AI trade: technology returned 57.8% and communication services 55.8% in 2023 versus 26.3% for the S&P 500, while utilities (-7.1%) were the worst sector as yields hit cycle highs. The March 2023 regional-bank crisis was contained by the BTFP; hyperscaler capex began its quadrupling.

regimes.name: Fed cuts, election and tariff shock
regimes.fed_policy: 50 bp cut on 18 September 2024, 25 bp in November and December 2024 to 4.25-4.5%, then on hold.
regimes.summary: Rate cuts and the AI-power narrative made utilities (+23.4%) and communication services (+40.2%) leaders in 2024, financials rallied on the election and deregulation hopes, and materials (0.0%) lagged. DeepSeek (27 January 2025) and then Liberation Day tariffs (2 April 2025) produced a 12% S&P 500 drawdown in four sessions, ending the regime at the 8 April low.

regimes.name: Tariff pause rally, AI capex and stablecoins
regimes.fed_policy: Hold until September 2025, then three cuts (17 September, 29 October, 10 December 2025) to 3.5-3.75%; QT ended with reserve-management bill purchases.
regimes.summary: The 9 April 2025 pause (S&P +9.52%) and chip exemptions drove a V-shaped recovery to a record on 27 June 2025 and a narrow AI leadership (Nvidia $5 trillion on 29 October). Gold more than doubled miners' value, the GENIUS Act and bank deregulation lifted fintech and banks, while software and IT services derated on AI-substitution fears. Communication services (+33.6%) led 2025; the S&P 500 returned 17.9%.

regimes.name: Iran war oil shock and the semiconductor melt-up
regimes.fed_policy: On hold at 3.5-3.75%; Powell under investigation, Kevin Warsh confirmed 13 May and sworn in 22 May 2026; first Warsh FOMC in June with no change.
regimes.summary: US-Israeli strikes on Iran (28 February), the closure of Hormuz and Brent at $119.50 (9 March) made energy the 2026 leader and gold spiked to about $5,400, while the Supreme Court's 20 February tariff ruling and replacement Section 122/301 duties cut the effective tariff rate. Semiconductors had their best quarter ever in Q2 (SMH +71%, SOX +106% year-to-date) on memory and CPU demand, even as software suffered the 'SaaS-pocalypse' and IT services derated.

regimes.name: AI credit stress, Fed hike and the midterm rotation
regimes.fed_policy: 25 bp hike to 3.75-4% on 16 September 2026 (first since July 2023), hold on 28 October with two dissents for a hike; markets price another hike in December.
regimes.ten_year_yield_range: approx. 4.5% to 4.9% (highest in years; some reports cite multi-decade highs in long yields)
regimes.summary: The 1 July semiconductor reversal, Alphabet's capex and free-cash-flow shocks (July and 29 October), CoreWeave's distressed bonds and CDS above 1,000 bp, state data-center moratoria and the 3 November Democratic sweep turned AI capex from growth story to credit question: XLK fell 19.2% in the month to 5 November 2026 while staples, health care and energy absorbed flows. Energy leads 2026 (+40.6%), communication services lags (-10.6%); the Nasdaq's 6 October record of 27,599.89 stands as the cycle high for now.
